newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - US March industry output seen up 0.6 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - US March industry output seen up 0.6 pct.

text.p: Strong U.S. manufacturing activity boosted U.S. industrial production in March, economists said, forecasting data which will neither surprise nor please U.S. credit markets.
In a Reuters poll, economists estimated that U.S. industrial production rose 0.6 percent last month after a 0.5 percent February increase.
Meanwhile, the portion of the nation's mines, utilities and factories utilized in that production rose to 83.6 in March, from 83.3 in February, the economists said.

"The March employment report, NAPM (National Association of Purchasing Management) and other indicators all point to another solid gain in the manufacturing sector," said Joshua Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "Capacity use will edge up a little, maybe get up above 83.5 -- nothing alarming," he said.

Sally Kleinman, economist at Chase Securities Inc., said output in all three sectors -- mines, utilities and manufacturing -- rose in March, but that the manufacturing sector was the "one largest contributor" to the gain.

Kleinman, forecasting a 0.6 percent gain in March industrial production and a rise to 83.5 percent in capacity utilization, said data contained in the March employment report suggested a good gain in manufacturing output.
"Total hours worked dropped, but manufacturing had a longer workweek," Kleinman said.
"An increase in actual manufacturing jobs and in hours worked suggest an increase in manufacturing output," she said.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell chief economist Ed Yardeni agreed, estimating a 0.6 percent jump in March industrial production and a rise in capacity utilization to 83.5 percent.

"The March employment report that came out earlier this month showed a big increase in overtime hours and overall hours worked in the manufacturing sector which is a good indication of another strong increase in industrial production," Yardeni said.

With all the foreshadowing of strong March industrial output that the markets have already received, a 0.6 percent rise should not come as a surprise to the market and therefore, ought not to set it back, analysts said. But a 0.6 percent rise in March industrial output after a 0.5 percent February gain, will not soothe the market either, they said.
"It's well anticipated that industrial production will be fairly strong, so a strong report might not elicit a very negative reaction from the bond market," said Feinman.
Yardeni said the output rise is not good news for the bond market, but he doubted the ability of the expected March gain to push the market still lower.

"It's not good for the credit markets," said Yardeni. "The Federal Reserve has made it clear that they want the economy to slow, so any signs that the economy is still strong are going to be worrisome for the bond market."
But Yardeni noted that the bond market has held steady at just under 7.20 percent on the 30-year bond yield.
"The bond market has discounted this news," he said. "There's not that much more downside."
